CALIFORNIA RESALE ROYALTIES ACT (CIVIL CODE § 986) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Untitled No. 4 · Jordan Lee

DECLARATION AND PURPOSE
This information sheet concerns a work titled Untitled No. 4, created by Jordan Lee (the “work”). Pat Morgan is identified here as the person reselling the work, and $45,000 and September 2, 2026 are identified here as the reported gross sale price and date of that resale, for reference only. This sheet summarizes provisions of California Civil Code § 986, sometimes called the California Resale Royalties Act, which as originally enacted required the seller of a work of fine art (or the seller's agent) to pay the work's artist a 5 percent royalty on specified California resales.

This sheet is an informational record only. It does not determine whether the resale identified above meets § 986's own definitions and conditions, does not determine whether any royalty is or was owed with respect to that resale, and does not itself assert, waive, calculate, or collect any royalty or other right under § 986 or any other law. As later sections of this sheet describe, federal courts have since held significant parts of § 986 unconstitutional or preempted by federal copyright law; this sheet is not legal advice and is not a substitute for reading the statute and that case law directly.

THE ROYALTY OBLIGATION, ITS WAIVER RULE, AND ASSIGNMENT
California Civil Code § 986(a), as enacted, states the core rule: “Whenever a work of fine art is sold and the seller resides in California or the sale takes place in California, the seller or the seller’s agent shall pay to the artist of such work of fine art or to such artist’s agent 5 percent of the amount of such sale.”

The statute makes the artist's right to that 5 percent difficult to waive down. It states: “The right of the artist to receive an amount equal to 5 percent of the amount of such sale may be waived only by a contract in writing providing for an amount in excess of 5 percent of the amount of such sale.”

The statute separately allows the artist to assign the right to collect the royalty, while preserving the same waiver limit: “An artist may assign the right to collect the royalty payment provided by this section to another individual or entity. However, the assignment shall not have the effect of creating a waiver prohibited by this subdivision.”

As written, subdivision (a) applies to a sale whenever either the seller resides in California or the sale takes place in California. As the next section of this sheet describes, a federal appellate court has since held the “seller resides in California” branch of that rule unconstitutional as applied to sales occurring entirely outside California.

HOW THE ROYALTY IS WITHHELD AND PAID
Subdivision (a)(1) places the withholding duty on the person who handles the sale on the seller's behalf: “When a work of fine art is sold at an auction or by a gallery, dealer, broker, museum, or other person acting as the agent for the seller the agent shall withhold 5 percent of the amount of the sale, locate the artist and pay the artist.”

Subdivision (a)(2) addresses what happens if the artist cannot be found: “If the seller or agent is unable to locate and pay the artist within 90 days, an amount equal to 5 percent of the amount of the sale shall be tranferred to the Arts Council.”

Subdivision (a)(5) then places a continuing duty on the Arts Council itself, and states what becomes of the money if the artist is never located: “The Arts Council shall attempt to locate any artist for whom money is received pursuant to this section. If the council is unable to locate the artist and the artist does not file a written claim for the money received by the council within seven years of the date of sale of the work of fine art, the right of the artist terminates and such money shall be transferred to the council for use in acquiring fine art pursuant to the Art in Public Buildings program set forth in Chapter 2.1 (commencing with Section 15813) of Part 10b of Division 3 of Title 2, of the Government Code.”

THE CIVIL ACTION THE STATUTE AUTHORIZES, AND ITS TIME LIMIT
Subdivision (a)(3) states the remedy for nonpayment and the deadline to pursue it: “If a seller or the seller’s agent fails to pay an artist the amount equal to 5 percent of the sale of a work of fine art by the artist or fails to transfer such amount to the Arts Council, the artist may bring an action for damages within three years after the date of sale or one year after the discovery of the sale, whichever is longer. The prevailing party in any action brought under this paragraph shall be entitled to reasonable attorney fees, in an amount as determined by the court.”

The prevailing party in any action brought under this paragraph shall be entitled to reasonable attorney fees, in an amount as determined by the court."

WHAT HAPPENS TO THE RIGHT AFTER THE ARTIST'S DEATH
Subdivision (a)(7) extends the right beyond the artist's lifetime, but only for artists who died after a specific date: “Upon the death of an artist, the rights and duties created under this section shall inure to his or her heirs, legatees, or personal representative, until the 20th anniversary of the death of the artist. The provisions of this paragraph shall be applicable only with respect to an artist who dies after January 1, 1983.”

Subdivision (b)(3) confirms that this is the only circumstance in which a post-death resale is covered: “Except as provided in paragraph (7) of subdivision (a), to a resale after the death of such artist.”

SALES THE STATUTE EXEMPTS
Subdivision (b) lists sales to which the royalty obligation in subdivision (a) does not apply. Among them: “To the initial sale of a work of fine art where legal title to such work at the time of such initial sale is vested in the artist thereof.”; “To the resale of a work of fine art for a gross sales price of less than one thousand dollars ($1,000).”; “To the resale of the work of fine art for a gross sales price less than the purchase price paid by the seller.”; “To the resale of a work of fine art by an art dealer to a purchaser within 10 years of the initial sale of the work of fine art by the artist to an art dealer, provided all intervening resales are between art dealers.”; and “To a sale of a work of stained glass artistry where the work has been permanently attached to real property and is sold as part of the sale of the real property to which it is attached.”

A separate exemption for a work of fine art exchanged for other fine art or property worth less than $1,000, and the post-death exemption addressed in this sheet's preceding clause, are also part of subdivision (b) but are not separately quoted here.

THE STATUTE'S DEFINITIONS OF “ARTIST,” “FINE ART,” AND “ART DEALER”
Subdivision (c) defines three terms the rest of the section depends on. Its own text states: “Artist” means the person who creates a work of fine art and who, at the time of resale, is a citizen of the United States, or a resident of the state who has resided in the state for a minimum of two years .

“Fine art” means an original painting, sculpture, or drawing, or an original work of art in glass.

“Art dealer” means a person who is actively and principally engaged in or conducting the business of selling works of fine art for which business such person validly holds a sales tax permit.

THE OUT-OF-STATE SALES CLAUSE WAS HELD UNCONSTITUTIONAL
Subdivision (a) applies “whenever a work of fine art is sold and the seller resides in California or the sale takes place in California.” Sitting en banc, the Ninth Circuit held that the first branch of that rule — reaching a sale merely because the seller resides in California, even when the sale itself happens entirely elsewhere — cannot stand: “we hold that the Act’s clause regulating sales outside the state of California facially violates the “dormant” Commerce Clause but that the offending provision is severable from the remainder of the Act.”

The court did not strike the statute in its entirety. It relied on the severability clause the Legislature itself wrote into the statute, Civil Code § 986(e): “If any provision of this section or the application thereof to any person or circumstance is held invalid for any reason, such invalidity shall not affect any other provisions or applications of this section which can be effected, without the invalid provision or application, and to this end the provisions of this section are severable.” Applying that clause, the court severed the unconstitutional “seller resides in California” branch and left the “sale takes place in California” branch of subdivision (a) standing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  "If any provision of this section or the application thereof to any person or circumstance is held invalid for any reason, such invalidity shall not affect any other provisions or applications of this section which can be effected, without the invalid provision or application, and to this end the provisions of this section are severable."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 986(e) (California Legislative Information), California Resale Royalties Act, the statute's own severability clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=986.)

POST-1978 RESALES ARE PREEMPTED BY FEDERAL COPYRIGHT LAW
In a later stage of the same litigation, the Ninth Circuit panel addressed a separate defect: whether the federal Copyright Act displaces § 986 entirely. The panel held that it does, for sales occurring on or after the effective date of the 1976 Copyright Act: “Plaintiffs’ CRRA claims covered by the 1976 Copyright Act—i.e., those concerning sales postdating the 1976 Act’s effective date of January 1, 1978—are expressly preempted by 17 U.S.C. § 301(a). We therefore affirm dismissal of those claims.”

The panel drew a narrow exception for a specific one-year window, because the earlier 1909 Copyright Act contained no comparable preemption provision: “The 1909 Copyright Act, however, has no express preemption provision. As such, plaintiffs’ CRRA claims covered only by the 1909 Act—i.e., those concerning sales that occurred between the CRRA’s effective date of January 1, 1977, and the 1976 Act’s effective date of January 1, 1978—cannot be expressly preempted.”

The panel summarized the practical effect of both rulings together: “Our decision today means that the CRRA had a short effective life. California’s statute permissibly coexisted for exactly one year alongside the 1909 Act.”

This sheet summarizes provisions of California Civil Code § 986, sometimes called the California Resale Royalties Act, which as originally enacted required the seller of a work of fine art (or the seller's agent) to pay the work's artist a 5 percent royalty on specified California resales.

As later sections of this sheet describe, federal courts have since held significant parts of § 986 unconstitutional or preempted by federal copyright law; this sheet is not legal advice and is not a substitute for reading the statute and that case law directly.

California Civil Code § 986(a), as enacted, states the core rule: “Whenever a work of fine art is sold and the seller resides in California or the sale takes place in California, the seller or the seller’s agent shall pay to the artist of such work of fine art or to such artist’s agent 5 percent of the amount of such sale.”

The statute makes the artist's right to that 5 percent difficult to waive down. It states: “The right of the artist to receive an amount equal to 5 percent of the amount of such sale may be waived only by a contract in writing providing for an amount in excess of 5 percent of the amount of such sale.”

The statute separately allows the artist to assign the right to collect the royalty, while preserving the same waiver limit: “An artist may assign the right to collect the royalty payment provided by this section to another individual or entity. However, the assignment shall not have the effect of creating a waiver prohibited by this subdivision.”

As written, subdivision (a) applies to a sale whenever either the seller resides in California or the sale takes place in California. As the next section of this sheet describes, a federal appellate court has since held the “seller resides in California” branch of that rule unconstitutional as applied to sales occurring entirely outside California.

Subdivision (a) applies “whenever a work of fine art is sold and the seller resides in California or the sale takes place in California.” Sitting en banc, the Ninth Circuit held that the first branch of that rule — reaching a sale merely because the seller resides in California, even when the sale itself happens entirely elsewhere — cannot stand: “we hold that the Act’s clause regulating sales outside the state of California facially violates the “dormant” Commerce Clause but that the offending provision is severable from the remainder of the Act.”

The court did not strike the statute in its entirety. It relied on the severability clause the Legislature itself wrote into the statute, Civil Code § 986(e): “If any provision of this section or the application thereof to any person or circumstance is held invalid for any reason, such invalidity shall not affect any other provisions or applications of this section which can be effected, without the invalid provision or application, and to this end the provisions of this section are severable.” Applying that clause, the court severed the unconstitutional “seller resides in California” branch and left the “sale takes place in California” branch of subdivision (a) standing.

In a later stage of the same litigation, the Ninth Circuit panel addressed a separate defect: whether the federal Copyright Act displaces § 986 entirely. The panel held that it does, for sales occurring on or after the effective date of the 1976 Copyright Act: “Plaintiffs’ CRRA claims covered by the 1976 Copyright Act—i.e., those concerning sales postdating the 1976 Act’s effective date of January 1, 1978—are expressly preempted by 17 U.S.C. § 301(a). We therefore affirm dismissal of those claims.”

The panel drew a narrow exception for a specific one-year window, because the earlier 1909 Copyright Act contained no comparable preemption provision: “The 1909 Copyright Act, however, has no express preemption provision. As such, plaintiffs’ CRRA claims covered only by the 1909 Act—i.e., those concerning sales that occurred between the CRRA’s effective date of January 1, 1977, and the 1976 Act’s effective date of January 1, 1978—cannot be expressly preempted.”

The panel summarized the practical effect of both rulings together: “Our decision today means that the CRRA had a short effective life. California’s statute permissibly coexisted for exactly one year alongside the 1909 Act.”
